/-!
# Erdős Problem 463

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/463](https://www.erdosproblems.com/463)
-/

@[expose] public section

open Filter

namespace Erdos463

/--
Is there a function $f$ with $f(n)\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$ such that,
for all large $n$, there is a composite number $m$ such that
$$
n + f(n) < m < n + p(m)
$$
Here $p(m)$ is the least prime factor of $m$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_463 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ (f : ℕ → ℕ) (_ : Tendsto f atTop atTop),
    ∀ᶠ n in atTop,
      ∃ m, m.Composite ∧
        n + f n < m ∧ m < n + m.minFac := by
  sorry

end Erdos463

reformulations.difference: The original formulation in Erdős–Graham (1980), p. 92, asks whether, for each fixed c and all n > n₀(c), there is a composite m > n+c with m−p(m) < n. Lean instead asks for one function f tending to infinity, with n+f(n) < m < n+p(m) eventually.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: A diverging f eventually exceeds each fixed c, giving the original assertion. Conversely, for each n choose the largest c ≤ n for which the required composite witness exists, using 0 if that finite set is empty. The source assertion makes the set nonempty eventually and makes the chosen values eventually exceed every fixed bound. Thus this choice supplies the required f. For composite m, minFac m ≤ m, so m−minFac m < n is equivalent to m < n+minFac m. The full equivalence was proved in /workspace/review/source_equivalence.lean without relying on sorryAx.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, Old and New Problems and Results in Combinatorial Number Theory (1980), p. 92 (PDF p. 88): https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf
https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/ — bibliography used to locate the original book

P. Erdős, Some Unconventional Problems in Number Theory, Mathematics Magazine 52 (1979), 67–70: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1979-22.pdf — examined while locating the original question; not the basis of the verdict

review.notes: The sole theorem's quantifiers, strict inequalities, composite restriction, least-prime-factor semantics, filters, and answer polarity are faithful. Small-value tests confirm that the exceptional minFac values at 0 and 1 cannot supply witnesses. Also proved equivalence with allowing real-valued f, by taking natural floors eventually.
